items.title: Abolish Lock Poisoning
items.author: Armin Ronacher
items.summary: Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex , the mutex is poisoned . That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError . The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state. items.title: The Explorer Pattern for product invention and development.
items.summary: tl;dr: the Explorer Pattern is one individual or team building a functional implementation that minimizes cross-team and cross-functional impacts as much as humanly possible, and then reconciling the details with other teams after that prototype is completed, accepting that this approach can require very substantial rework to that initial development. Why write this? Imprint previously called this the “Tech-led” or “Engineering-led” development model, but it’s pretty unclear to folks what that means. items.title: Data Contracts
items.author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
items.summary: Data contracts are a way to describe the contents and guarantees of datasets. Simon Harrer and Arif Wider describe in detail what they are and how to use them. They apply practices from API design to data by treating them as data-providing services - such as data products - whose interfaces we want to define as clearly as possible. This approach significantly increases the robustness of large-scale data landscapes, and gives both people and AI agents the explicit, trustworthy metadata they need to work with data autonomously, which is why more and more enterprises are adopting them. more…

items.title: Deterministic Simulation Testing
items.author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
items.summary: Distributed systems are hard to test because partial failures overlap with live traffic and the same fault can produce different execution traces on different runs. Unmesh Joshi describes how deterministic simulation testing addresses this by replacing real clocks, networks, and storage with simulated components driven by a single-threaded execution loop. This allows simulating both hard failures and routine slowdowns—such as network and disk latency spikes—and more importantly makes every execution reproducible. items.title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.summary: When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances. items.title: Tests as data: ensuring AI-generated code does what we want
items.author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
items.summary: Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors. Matteo Vaccari makes three claims: (1) when AI writes the code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3) moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this optimizes for human-readable tests

items.title: Long-horizon agents and durable execution
items.author: Martin Fowler (martin@martinfowler.com)
items.summary: Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior. Kiran Prakash explains durable execution: an emerging pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards their goal. items.title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
items.author: Rachel Laycock (rlaycock@thoughtworks.com)
items.summary: TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well.
